subject: english
stem: The commander gave a terse reply. As used here, "terse" most nearly means
rationale: Terse means short and to the point. B is the item's whole reason for existing: terse carries a faint suggestion of curtness, so candidates who have absorbed the tone without the meaning reach for "angry". The denotation is brevity, and a terse reply can be perfectly good-humoured. A and D are unrelated.

subject: english
stem: Which word is most nearly the opposite of "scarce"?
rationale: Scarce means in short supply, so its opposite is plentiful. A is the strongest distractor because it is what scarcity causes rather than what it means — things become expensive because they are scarce, which makes "expensive" feel connected while being neither a synonym nor an antonym. Confusing a consequence with a definition is the error being tested.

subject: english
stem: Choose the correct word: Neither of the boys ___ finished the work.
rationale: "Neither" is singular and governs the verb; "of the boys" is a prepositional phrase that does not. B is the dominant error and the point of the item — the plural noun sits directly next to the verb and pulls the ear towards "have". C is not a finite verb at all. A is plural and in the wrong tense.

subject: english
stem: Choose the correct word: The soldier was accused ___ neglecting his duty.
rationale: "Accused of" is the fixed collocation in English. B is the common error, borrowed from the pattern of "blamed for" and "punished for", which take a different preposition for a closely related idea. Collocations cannot be reasoned out from meaning, which is what makes this a test of exposure to the language rather than of logic.

subject: english
stem: The captain told the cadets to pull up their socks. He was telling them to
rationale: The idiom means to make a greater effort. B is the literal reading and is exactly what the item is looking for — a candidate who has never met the phrase will translate it word by word, and the literal sense is plausible enough in a parade-ground setting to feel safe. A and D are contextually reasonable orders that the idiom does not mean.

subject: english
stem: Thermometer is to temperature as barometer is to
rationale: The relation is instrument to the quantity it measures, and a barometer measures atmospheric pressure. A is why this sits at moderate rather than easy: weather is what a barometer is popularly used to predict, so the association is strong and the candidate has to notice that predicting is not measuring. C is a derived reading, D belongs to a hygrometer. Distinguishing the stated relation from a merely strong association is the skill.

subject: english
stem: Pointing to a photograph, Ravi said, "She is the daughter of the only son of my father." How is the girl related to Ravi?
rationale: The only son of Ravi's father is Ravi himself, so the girl is his daughter. The phrase has to be unwound from the inside out, and B is what a candidate lands on by stopping one step early at "my father's daughter". A comes from slipping a generation. Deliberately phrased as "the only son of my father" rather than "my grandfather's only son", which is ambiguous — that version leaves open whether the speaker descends through the son or a daughter, and admits two defensible answers.

subject: english
stem: The library was silent except for the scratch of pens. Anand glanced at the clock, closed his unopened book and left. It is most reasonable to conclude that Anand
rationale: Two details carry it: the glance at the clock, and the book being unopened. Together they say he never began and something about the hour ended it. C is the trap and it is contradicted by a single word — "unopened" — which a candidate skimming for the gist will pass straight over. Moderate because the evidence is in the adjectives rather than the action.

subject: english
stem: "We should cancel the outdoor parade. The forecast says heavy rain." This argument assumes that
rationale: For the forecast to be a reason to cancel, rain must matter to the parade — remove that and the argument collapses, which is the test of a genuine assumption. A is the sharpest distractor: the argument does need the forecast to be reasonably reliable, but "never wrong" is far stronger than anything required, and an assumption that overshoots is not the one being made. Separating necessary from merely agreeable is what puts this at moderate.

subject: english
stem: Choose the word that best joins these sentences: The cadet trained every morning. ___, he failed the fitness test.
rationale: Training every morning ought to predict passing, so the second sentence reverses the expectation and needs a connector of contrast. B asserts the opposite relation and is the dominant error, chosen by candidates who register that the sentences are linked without registering how. C adds, A illustrates; neither fits a reversal. The item tests whether the candidate reads the relation between sentences or only their subject matter.

subject: english
stem: In a race, Amit finished ahead of Bhavna. Chetan finished behind Bhavna but ahead of Dev. Ravi finished ahead of Amit. Who finished third?
rationale: The constraints give Ravi, Amit, Bhavna, Chetan, Dev in that order, so third is Bhavna. Difficult because no single statement fixes a position — the order only emerges once all four are combined, and the final clause moves Ravi above Amit after the reader has probably already settled Amit at the top. A is what you get by stopping before that clause.

subject: english
stem: "Not all cadets passed the swimming test." Which statement must be true?
rationale: Negating "all passed" establishes one exception and nothing more. C is the distractor that catches most candidates: "not all" is heard in speech as "rather few", when it is satisfied by a single failure among a hundred passes. B confuses "not all" with "none". Difficult because ordinary usage and strict logic pull apart, and the item rewards the strict reading.

subject: english
stem: "Students who eat breakfast score higher in exams, so eating breakfast improves exam scores." Which finding would most weaken this argument?

options.A: Some students dislike eating in the morning
options.B: Breakfast is cheap and widely available
options.C: Students who eat breakfast also sleep more
options.D: Exam scores have risen over ten years

rationale: The argument reads a correlation as a cause. C supplies a third factor that could produce both the breakfast and the better scores, which is what undermines a causal claim — the strongest attack is an alternative explanation, not a denial of the data. B is irrelevant, A limits the remedy without touching the reasoning, D describes an unrelated trend. Difficult because the candidate must locate the argument's structure before judging the options.

subject: english
stem: A town banned cars from its centre. Shops in the centre reported higher sales; shops just outside reported lower sales. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.A: Shoppers shifted from one area to another
options.B: The ban raised total sales across the town
options.C: The ban harmed every local shop
options.D: Cars never affected shopping at all

rationale: One area rose while its neighbour fell, which is the signature of redistribution rather than growth — nothing here measures the total. B is the overreach the item is built around: it reports only the good half of the evidence and is the conclusion an advocate of the ban would announce. C ignores the shops that gained. Difficult because both halves of the data have to be held together, and the tempting answer uses one of them.

subject: english
stem: "The new rifle is lighter than the old one, and cheaper. Reliability tests are still under way." The writer's attitude to the new rifle is best described as
rationale: Two advantages are stated plainly and then held in check by an unresolved question, which is approval with a reservation attached. D takes the praise and discards the final sentence; A takes the flat, factual register as an absence of any view, missing that the writer has chosen to lead with two advantages. Difficult because tone here is carried by what is placed last rather than by any evaluative word.
